observation.visible_scene: A close-up, eye-level view of a dining table. A white ceramic mug sits centered in the foreground on a bamboo-slat placemat; to its right is an empty white plate, and to its left a metal knife rests on a folded red napkin. The background is out of focus, showing an open doorway, a dark kitchen appliance with a bright white square panel, and an upholstered chair. A column of pale steam/vapor rises continuously from the mouth of the mug throughout the clip.
visible_changes: The steam plume above the mug rim changes shape and vertical extent from frame to frame while the mug, plate, knife, placemat and all background elements stay in fixed screen positions.
Early frames (t=0.00–0.13) show a thin, gently wavy vertical ribbon of vapor directly above the rim.
Around t=0.20–0.40 a compact, rounded puff/vortex-like blob forms just above the rim and then begins to drift upward.
In the middle frames (t=0.47–1.20) that puff elongates and curls as it rises, with a faint separate wispy trail appearing higher up (visible near the top of the frame around t=0.87–1.20).
Later frames (t=1.33–2.00) show a broader, more turbulent cloud of vapor with darker, broken wisps hugging the rim.
Toward the end (t=2.07–2.67) the vapor thins again into curling ribbons that rise and lean slightly to the left above the mug.
The motion observed is deformation plus upward translation of the vapor; no solid object moves, and no new object enters or leaves the scene.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the mug contains a hot liquid (the interior contents are not visible) and what produced the steam.
The cause of the curling/turbulence in the vapor (air currents, temperature gradients, etc.).
What happens to the steam before t=0 and after t=2.67; the excerpt is a temporal crop with the rising process already underway at the start and still continuing at the end.
uncertain_details: Camera motion: the background and table objects remain at constant screen positions, so the camera appears static, but this is inferred only from the fixed solids.
The exact fluid-dynamic character of each puff (vortex ring vs. simple curl) cannot be determined from the frames.
The thin high wisps in some frames may be the same vapor column seen against the bright background rather than a distinct second plume.

may already be underway in the first view and may continue beyond the last. The endpoints need
NOT match or connect as a loop. Do not judge different endpoints as a physical inconsistency,
and do not invent a trigger, contact, start, stop, landing, disappearance or completion to make
the excerpt form a complete story. Missing context outside this segment stays unknown.
If an editing cut is visible inside the segment, distinguish it from continuous physical motion;
do not invent a smooth transition or a causal mechanism to connect the two views.
Describe what is visible during the excerpt, the actual changes, and supported persistent
properties. Cover the main visible process, not just scenery. Distinguish object movement from
camera movement, reflection from separate objects, expansion from translation, deformation from
occlusion, and an already ongoing process from its onset. Only state what the clip supports;
do not invent causes, an earlier impact, an unseen operator, material identities or later outcomes.
Do not infer motion from one frame, a visible seam or a single pose. Static intervals are valid.
Do not supply named physics laws. Compare each important entity's first and last image positions
and their relative positions before describing motion. Treat camera motion as uncertain when the
background evidence is insufficient, and retain clear relative changes despite that uncertainty.
Return JSON {"visible_scene":"...", "visible_changes":["observation supported within the excerpt"],
